title: Whose image? (Matthew 22:15–46)
hookLine: a coin with a face on it, and a question about whose face is on you
tomorrow: if Jesus said call no man father, why do some churches?

cards: Pull a coin from a pocket or a jar and look: there's often a face on it. Here's yesterday's question. Some of Jesus' opponents bring him a trap.
Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not? Say pay, and he sides with Rome. Say don't, and Rome hears it.
He asks to see the coin. "Whose is this image and superscription?" Caesar's, they say.
"Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's." They marvel, and leave.

teach.b: The coin carries Caesar's image, so give it back to him. What carries God's image? Genesis says God created man "in his own image."
On that reading, the coin goes to Caesar, and the person holding it belongs to God.

teach.h: ONE ANCESTOR, SO NONE IS GREATER.
teach.b: That verse is Jewish scripture first, and a teaching in the Mishnah draws a striking lesson from it: God began humankind with one person, so that no one could say to another, my ancestor was greater than yours.

One image, one family. Then more questions come. To the lawyer who asks for the greatest commandment, Jesus answers from the Torah: love God with all your heart, soul and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself.
"On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets."
By the end, Matthew says, nobody dared ask him anything more.

how: Christians quote 'render unto Caesar' when they talk about faith and government, and some churches recite the two great commandments, love of God and of neighbor, as a summary of the law.

o: Jesus' question about the face on a coin
a test of who could draw the best portrait
a riddle about which king built the temple

games.q: questions in the temple — tap the pairs.
p: God created man in his own image
one ancestor, so none is greater

s: render unto Caesar means money is unholy
he says give Caesar what bears Caesar's image, and God what is God's. the coin isn't called evil.
both great commandments come from Jewish scripture
love God (Deuteronomy) and love your neighbor (Leviticus): Jesus answers from the Torah.
Jesus refused to answer the question about taxes
he asked for the coin and answered: render unto Caesar, and unto God.

games.q: your friend says real faith means refusing to pay taxes, since everything belongs to God. what did Jesus do with the coin?
o: said give Caesar's to Caesar, and God's to God.
said all money is God's, so refuse the tax.
said nothing, and walked out of the temple.
games.why: Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's. both, not either.

practice: Hold a coin, or any bill, and look at the face on it for a few breaths. Then set it down, turn your own hand over, and look at it the same way: the lines, the knuckles, the pulse at the wrist.
In Genesis, that's where the other image is.

wordCard.voice: Whose image? Jesus' question over a coin: Caesar's face on the money, and, some readers add, God's on the one holding it.

orig.note: Greek for image, on the coin in Matthew 22:20: whose is this image?

carryVoice: Your line: render unto God, the things, and the people, that bear his image. Two weeks, done.
